'''Sir Alan Rushton Battersby''' (4 March 1925 – 10 February 2018) was an English [[organic chemist]] best known for his work to define the chemical intermediates in the biosynthetic pathway to [[Vitamin B12|vitamin B<sub>12</sub>]] and the [[reaction mechanism]]s of the [[enzymes]] involved. His research group was also notable for its [[organic synthesis|synthesis]] of [[radiolabelled]] precursors to study [[alkaloid]] biosynthesis and the [[stereochemistry]] of [[Enzyme catalysis|enzymic reactions]]. He won numerous awards including the [[Royal Medal]] in 1984 and the [[Copley Medal]] in 2000. He was knighted in the [[1992 New Year Honours]]. Battersby died in February 2018 at the age of 92.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.caths.cam.ac.uk/about-us/news-and-events/professor-sir-alan-battersby-1925-2018 |title= Professor Sir Alan Battersby (1925-2018) |publisher=[[St Catharine's College, Cambridge]] |access-date= 2018-05-01}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Alan Battersby was born in [[Leigh, Lancashire]], on 4 March 1925, one of three children of William Battersby, a master plumber, and his wife Hilda née Rushton.<ref name=ODNB>{{cite book |doi=10.1093/odnb/9780198614128.013.90000380419 |chapter=Battersby, Sir Alan Rushton (1925–2018), organic chemist |title=Oxford Dictionary of National Biography |year=2022 |last1=Leeper |first1=Finian |last2=McDonald |first2=Ted |isbn=978-0-19-861412-8 }}</ref> At the age of 11 he entered [[Leigh Grammar School]], where his chemistry teacher, Mr Evans, nurtured and encouraged him. He would have continued his schooling into the sixth form but for the fact that by age sixteen the [[Second World War]] was underway and he decided that he should join the war effort by working for [[British Insulated Callender's Cables|BICC]] in their local factory. He soon concluded that this decision had been a mistake and so used his spare time to study independently at Salford Technical College for the [[Higher School Certificate (England and Wales)|Higher School Certificate]] that would be required to enter university.<ref name=ODNB/><ref name=LaterLife>{{Cite web|title=Sir Alan Battersby's 90th Birthday Celebrations|url=http://www.caths.cam.ac.uk/about-us/news-and-events/unveiling-portrait-professor-sir-alan-battersby-and-his-90th-birthday | date =2015-03-21 |access-date=2018-05-01 |publisher=[[St Catharine's College, Cambridge]] }}</ref><ref name=TimesObituary>{{cite news|title=Battersby's obituary in ''The Times'' newspaper|url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/professor-sir-alan-battersby-obituary-33pbccbhw | date =2018-02-03 |access-date=2018-05-01|newspaper=[[The Times]]}}</ref>
In October 1943, Battersby took up his place at the [[University of Manchester]]'s Chemistry Department, having won a scholarship to support his undergraduate studies. He graduated with first class honours in 1946 and that year obtained a Mercer Chemistry Research Scholarship (named in honour of [[John Mercer (scientist)|John Mercer]]) and a [[Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (United Kingdom)|DSIR]] grant. These awards allowed him to complete an MSc (Manchester) in 1947 under the supervision of Dr Hal T Openshaw. When Openshaw was appointed as a [[Reader (academic rank)|Reader]] at the [[University of St Andrews]], they both moved there and Battersby completed his PhD, which was awarded in 1949.<ref name=thesis>{{cite thesis |last=Battersby |first=Alan R. |date=1949 |title=Researches into the structure of Emetine |type=PhD |publisher=[[University of St Andrews]] |hdl=10023/11240 }}</ref> He was immediately appointed an assistant lecturer at St Andrews.<ref name=LaterLife/> This first appointment extended from 1949 to 1953 but was interrupted by two years owing to a [[Harkness Fellowship|Commonwealth Fund Fellowship]] he obtained for post-doctoral study in the United States. The first year was spent with [[Lyman C. Craig]] at the [[Rockefeller University|Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research]], [[New York City|New York]], working on the [[peptide]] [[antibiotics]] [[tyrocidine]] and [[gramicidin S]]. The second year involved a move to the [[biochemistry]] department of the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign|University of Illinois]], working with [[H. E. Carter|Herbert Carter]] on [[Pyruvate oxidase|pyruvate oxidation factor]].<ref name=RSCbiog>{{Cite journal |url= http://pubs.rsc.org/-/content/articlehtml/2013/ob/c3ob90109b?page=search |title= Brief biography of A R Battersby |year= 2013 |publisher= [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] |doi= 10.1039/C3OB90109B |pmid= 23963504 |access-date= 2018-05-01 |last1= Thompson |first1= S. |last2= Wilson |first2= A. J. |last3= Battersby |first3= A. R. |journal= Organic & Biomolecular Chemistry |volume= 11 |issue= 37 |pages= 6236–6241 |archive-date= 11 May 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180511215024/http://pubs.rsc.org/-/content/articlehtml/2013/ob/c3ob90109b?page=search |url-status= dead |url-access= subscription }}</ref><ref name=cam1702>{{Cite book|title=The 1702 chair of chemistry at Cambridge: transformation and change|editor1-first=Mary D. |editor1-last=Archer |editor-link=Mary Archer |editor2-first= Christopher D. |editor2-last=Haley |last = Battersby | first = Alan |chapter= Chapter 11: Discovering the wonder of how Nature builds its molecules |pages=xvi, 257–282 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2005 |isbn=0-521-82873-2}}</ref>{{efn|Reference <ref name=cam1702/> is, in effect, Sir Alan Battersby's [[autobiography]]. Initially drafted in 2002 for a departmental symposium, it provides a candid account of his scientific journey from childhood to old age. The expanded book chapter published in 2005 was "written for the non-specialist audience" and includes many insights into the choices and decisions he made, for example to switch from alkaloid chemistry to the "pigments of life".}}

== Later career ==
In 1954, Battersby was appointed a lecturer at the University of Bristol, where he stayed until 1962. This was the period when his own research group of doctoral and post-doctoral students became established. In 1962 he was appointed as a professor of chemistry at [[University of Liverpool|Liverpool University]] until, in 1969, he moved to a professorship at the [[University of Cambridge]] and became a [[Fellow]] of [[St Catharine's College, Cambridge|St Catharine's College]]. At the time, this was the second Chair of Organic Chemistry at the university, created especially for him; [[Lord Todd]] then held the first. In 1988, Professor Battersby was elected to the prestigious [[BP Professor of Organic Chemistry|1702 Chair of Chemistry]] in his [[Department of Chemistry, University of Cambridge|department]] and held that post until his retirement in 1992 when he was granted [[emeritus]] status within his college and department, reflecting his distinguished service.<ref name=RSCbiog/><ref name=cam1702/><ref name=DeptObit>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ch.cam.ac.uk/news/remembering-sir-alan-battersby|title=Remembering Sir Alan Battersby |publisher=[[Department of Chemistry, University of Cambridge]]|access-date=2018-05-01}}</ref>

== Research ==
The full output of Battersby's work has been published in over 350, mainly [[peer review|peer-reviewed]], articles.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://academictree.org/chemistry/publications.php?pid=56320&searchstring=&showfilter=all |title=Alan Rushton Battersby publications |access-date=2020-07-21 |publisher=Academictree.org}}</ref> His research, particularly at Cambridge, took a very collaborative approach which was necessary given the extended time period of the ambitious projects undertaken. Aside from his postgraduate and post-doctoral students, who participated typically for one to three years, the Battersby group included other members of the academic staff of the department, notably [[Department of Chemistry, University of Cambridge|Jim Staunton]], Ted McDonald and [[Department of Chemistry, University of Cambridge|Finian Leeper]].<ref name=journals>{{Cite web|url=https://scholar.google.co.uk/scholar?start=330&q=author:%22a+r+battersby%22&hl=en&as_sdt=1,5&as_vis=1 |title=Google Scholar results for A R Battersby}}</ref>
The group was funded by external grants, including those from the [[Science and Engineering Research Council|SERC]], the [[EPSRC]], the [[Leverhulme Trust]], [[Hoffman-La Roche]], the [[Wolfson Foundation]] and [[Zeneca]].<ref name=journals/>

=== Alkaloids ===
[[Alkaloid]]s are a group of naturally occurring chemical compounds that mostly contain [[Base (chemistry)|basic]] [[nitrogen]] atoms. They have a wide range of [[pharmacology|pharmacological activities]] which has made them of considerable interest to researchers. Prior to the 1950s, experimentation, often involving [[chemical degradation]] and partial or complete synthesis of possible structures, was necessary to determine their [[structural formula|chemical identity]] which, owing to their [[stereochemistry]], was often difficult to fully describe.<ref>{{cite book | last1=Manske | first1=R. H. F. | last2=Holmes | first2=H. L. | title=The Alkaloids: Chemistry and Physiology | publisher=Elsevier Science & Technology | publication-place=Saint Louis |orig-year=1952 | date=2014 | isbn=978-1-4832-2197-7 }}</ref> This, for example, was the case for [[emetine]], used for the treatment of [[Amoebiasis|amoebic infections]] and the subject of Battersby's PhD thesis.<ref name=thesis/> As he later commented<ref name=cam1702/><blockquote>"Roughly 100 g of emetine had been consumed in this work; modern tools would allow the structure of emetine to be determined in three days at most using about 10 mg of recoverable material (365 times faster using 10,000 times less material)."</blockquote>
These tools are the now-familiar [[mass spectrometry]], multi-atom [[nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy]] and [[X-ray crystallography]]: when applied to alkaloids these allowed relationships in structural sub-types to be clarified. This meant that attention could switch to an understanding of the biosynthetic pathways by which these materials are produced in the [[bacteria]], [[fungi]], [[plants]] and [[animals]] in which they are found. In 1937, Sonderhoff and Thomas showed how [[deuterium]]-labelled acetate could be used to investigate the biosynthesis of fats and steroids;<ref>{{cite journal | title=Die enzymatische Dehydrierung der Trideutero-essigsaure |last1=Sonderhoff | first1=R. |last2=Thomas | first2=H. | journal =Liebigs Ann. Chem. | year =1937 |volume=530 | pages =195–213 |doi=10.1002/jlac.19375300116}}</ref> by 1950 [[carbon-13|<sup>13</sup>C]] and [[carbon-14|<sup>14</sup>C]] labelled acetate had been incorporated into [[cholesterol]].<ref>{{cite journal | title=Studies on the utilization of acetic acid for the biological synthesis of cholesterol. |last1=Little | first1=H. N. |last2=Bloch | first2=K. | journal =J. Biol. Chem. | year =1950 |volume=183 | pages =33–46 |doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(18)56441-3 |url=http://www.jbc.org/content/183/1/33.short| doi-access=free }}</ref> Battersby realised that these techniques could be used to study alkaloid biosynthesis and that it was timely to do so because simple one-carbon precursors had become commercially available. By using [[radiolabelled]] starting materials incorporating [[tritium]] or, especially, <sup>14</sup>C to follow intermediates on the pathway, he determined the sequence in which the multiple alkaloids found together in a given organism were formed. For example, the biosynthesis of [[morphine]] was shown to proceed from L-[[tyrosine]] via [[reticuline]], [[salutaridine]], [[thebaine]], [[codeinone]] and [[codeine]].<ref>{{cite journal | title=Investigations on the Biosynthesis of Morphine Alkaloids |last1 = Barton | first1 = D. H. R. |last2= Battersby | first2 = A. R. |display-authors=etal | journal =J. Chem. Soc.  | year =1965 |volume = 65 | pages =2423–2438 |doi=10.1039/JR9650002423|pmid = 14288334 }}</ref><ref name=tritium>{{cite journal | title=Applications of tritium labeling for the exploration of biochemical mechanisms |last=Battersby | first= Alan R. | journal =Acc. Chem. Res. | year =1972 |volume=5 |issue=4 | pages =148–154 |doi=10.1021/ar50052a005}}</ref> The Battersby group worked on many other alkaloids, for example [[colchicine]], (from the autumn crocus ''[[Colchicum autumnale]]'') which is used to treat [[gout]]. This was shown to be derived from the amino acids [[phenylalanine]] and [[tyrosine]] via (S)-autumnaline.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scholar.google.co.uk/scholar?as_q=colchicine&as_epq=&as_oq=&as_eq=&as_occt=title&as_sauthors=%22ar+battersby%22&as_publication=&as_ylo=&as_yhi=&hl=en&as_sdt=1%2C5&as_vis=1 |title=Battersby group papers about colchicine}}</ref> Similarly, the biosynthesis of the [[indole alkaloids]] [[ajmalicine]], [[corynantheal]], [[catharanthine]] and [[vindoline]] was shown to involve the precursors [[tryptamine]] and [[loganin]].<ref>{{cite journal | title=The biosynthesis of plant alkaloids and nitrogenous microbial metabolites |last=Herbert | first= Richard B. | journal =Nat. Prod. Rep. | year =2001 |volume=18 |issue=1 | pages =50–65 |doi=10.1039/A809393H|pmid=11245400 }}</ref> To Alan Battersby's surprise, [[quinine]], the [[anti-malarial]] drug was shown to derive from corynantheal, although it does not share its [[indole]] substructure.<ref name=cam1702/>

=== Biosynthesis of the "Pigments of Life" ===
[[File:ARBLecturing.jpg|thumb|Prof Alan Battersby lecturing on porphyrin biosynthesis.]]
Battersby is, above all, known for his research on the biosynthesis of the "pigments of life" that are built on closely related [[tetrapyrrole|tetrapyrrolic structural frameworks]]. His research group elucidated, in particular, the essential role played by two enzymes, [[Porphobilinogen deaminase|deaminase]] and [[uroporphyrinogen III synthase|cosynthetase]], in the steps from [[aminolevulinic acid]] via [[porphobilinogen]] and [[hydroxymethylbilane]] to [[uroporphyrinogen III]]. The latter is the first [[macrocycle|macrocyclic]] intermediate in the [[biosynthesis]] of [[heme|haem]], [[chlorophyll]], [[vitamin B12|vitamin B<sub>12</sub>]] (cobalamin), [[siroheme|sirohaem]] and [[cofactor F430]]. The work involved the careful study of labelled intermediates, using [[deuterium]], [[tritium]], [[carbon-13|<sup>13</sup>C]] and [[carbon-14|<sup>14</sup>C]] placed into potential precursors made by [[organic synthesis|organic]] or [[enzyme|enzyme-assisted]] synthesis. The most successful strategy was to incorporate the stable isotope <sup>13</sup>C into potential substrates, since the outcome of the biochemical reactions (for example giving [[uroporphyrinogen III]]) could readily be followed using high-field [[Carbon-13 nuclear magnetic resonance|<sup>13</sup>C NMR]]. The Battersby group's use of doubly-<sup>13</sup>C-labelled [[porphobilinogen]] was especially revealing of the rearrangement step which had puzzled those who wished to understand the details of the biosynthesis of uroporphyrinogen III.<ref>{{cite journal | title=Biosynthesis of the pigments of life: formation of the macrocycle |last1=Battersby | first1= Alan R. |last2=Fookes | first2=Christopher J. R. |last3=Matcham | first3=George W.J. |last4=McDonald | first4=Edward | journal =Nature | year =1980 |volume=285 |issue=5759 | pages =17–21 |doi=10.1038/285017a0|pmid=6769048 |bibcode=1980Natur.285...17B |s2cid=9070849 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | title=Anaerobic synthesis of vitamin B12: characterization of the early steps in the pathway |last1=Frank | first1= S. |display-authors=et al | journal =Biochemical Society Transactions  | year =2005 |volume=33 |issue=4 | pages =811–814 |doi=10.1042/BST0330811|pmid=16042604 }}</ref> Based on these results, Battersby suggested that a spiro-pyrrolenine intermediate was generated at the active site of cosynthetase and to prove this mechanism his group designed and synthesised a spiro-lactam analogue which was indeed shown to inhibit the enzyme.<ref>{{cite journal | title=Biosynthesis of Porphyrins and Related Macrocycles. Part 40. Synthesis of a Spiro-lactam Related to the Proposed Spiro-intermediate for Porphyrin Biosynthesis: Inhibition of Cosynthetase  |last1=Stark | first1=W. M. |last2=Hawker | first2=C. J. |display-authors=et al | journal =J. Chem. Soc., Perkin Trans. 1 | year =1993 | pages =2875–2892 |doi=10.1039/P19930002875 | issue=23}}</ref>
[[File: ARB office portrait2.jpg |thumb |Prof Alan Battersby in his office in the [[Department of Chemistry, University of Cambridge|Cambridge department]].]]
Later steps towards vitamin B<sub>12</sub>, especially the incorporation of the additional methyl groups of its structure, were investigated using methyl-labelled [[S-adenosyl methionine]]. It was not until a [[genetic engineering|genetically engineered]] strain of ''[[Pseudomonas denitrificans]]'' was used, in which eight of the genes involved in the [[biosynthesis of cobalamin]] had been [[gene expression|overexpressed]], that the complete sequence of methylation and other steps could be determined thus fully establishing all the intermediates in the pathway.<ref name=cam1702/><ref name=Bakerian>{{cite journal| title=Biosynthesis of the pigments of life |last = Battersby | first = A. R. | journal =Proc. R. Soc. Lond. B  | year =1985 | volume = 225 |issue = 1238 | pages =1–26 |doi=10.1098/rspb.1985.0047|pmid = 2863821 |s2cid = 2022475 }}</ref>
<ref>{{cite journal| title=How Nature builds the pigments of life |last = Battersby | first = A. R. | journal =Pure and Applied Chemistry  | year =1993 | volume = 65 |issue = 6 | pages =1113–1122 |url=https://www.degruyter.com/downloadpdf/j/pac.1993.65.issue-6/pac199365061113/pac199365061113.pdf  |doi=10.1351/pac199365061113|s2cid = 83942303 }}</ref>
<ref>{{cite journal| title=Tetrapyrroles: the Pigments of Life. A Millennium review |last = Battersby | first = A. R. | journal =Nat. Prod. Rep.  | year =2000 | volume = 17 |issue = 6 | pages =507–526 |doi=10.1039/B002635M | pmid = 11152419}}</ref>
As Battersby wrote in his review article in ''Accounts of Chemical Research''<ref>{{cite journal| title=Biosynthesis of vitamin B12 |last = Battersby | first = Alan R. | journal =Acc. Chem. Res.  | year =1993 | volume = 26 | pages =15–21 |doi=10.1021/ar00025a003}}</ref>
<blockquote>"One can get some appreciation of the massive effort that was involved by the groups of [[Duilio Arigoni|Arigoni]], Battersby, Francis Blanche, Vladimir Bykhovski, Joel Crouzet, Gerhard Muller and A. Ian Scott; K. Bernhauer and David Shemin also made some early contributions." </blockquote>

=== Haem natural products and mimics ===
[[File: Laboratory 122 Cambridge Chemistry.jpg |thumb |This is a typical laboratory bench used by a PhD student in the Battersby group in 1976. It was located in Lab 122 of the [[Department of Chemistry, University of Cambridge|chemistry department]].]]
The Battersby group's work on the biosynthesis of haem-related [[natural products]] involved considerable [[organic synthesis]]. For example, they produced fully synthetic [[heme a|haem a]],<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1039/P19850000135 |title=Isolation, crystallisation, and synthesis of the dimethyl ester of porphyrin a, the iron-free prosthetic group of cytochrome c oxidase |year=1985 |last1=Battersby |first1=Alan R. |last2=McDonald |first2=Edward |last3=Thompson |first3=Mervyn |last4=Chaudhry |first4=Irshad A. |last5=Clezy |first5=Peter S. |last6=Fookes |first6=Christopher J. R. |last7=Hai |first7=Ton That |journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Perkin Transactions 1 |pages=135 }}</ref> [[haem d1]]<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1039/A700655A |title=Haem d1: Stereoselective synthesis of the macrocycle to establish its absolute configuration as 2R,7R 1 |year=1997 |last1=Micklefield |first1=Jason |last2=Beckmann |first2=Marion |last3=MacKman |first3=Richard L. |last4=Block |first4=Michael H. |last5=Leeper |first5=Finian J. |last6=Battersby |first6=Alan R. |journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Perkin Transactions 1 |issue=14 |pages=2123–2138 }}
</ref> and [[sirohydrochlorin]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1039/C39850001061 |title=Syntheses relevant to vitamin B12 biosynthesis: Synthesis of sirohydrochlorin and of its octamethyl ester |year=1985 |last1=Block |first1=Michael H. |last2=Zimmerman |first2=Steven C. |last3=Henderson |first3=Graeme B. |last4=Turner |first4=Simon P. D. |last5=Westwood |first5=Steven W. |last6=Leeper |first6=Finian J. |last7=Battersby |first7=Alan R. |journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Chemical Communications |issue=16 |pages=1061 }}</ref> Another challenge requiring pure synthesis was to investigate the function of the [[enzyme]]s that contained porphyrin-related ligands, or (in the case of [[hemoglobin|haemoglobin]]) used haem for [[oxygen]]-transport, by [[Enzyme mimic|mimicking]] these properties without recourse to the [[protein]] that in nature surrounds the [[active site]]. Battersby chose to investigate mimics for [[myoglobin]] and [[cytochrome P450]], designing artificial targets wherein a single metal-containing [[coordination complex]] was synthesised and its behaviour compared with the natural system it was replacing. The small-molecule targets were porphyrins carrying substituents in positions where they would be unlikely to interfere with the electronic properties of the metal complex. By the time that he retired in 1992, this area of chemistry had become very active.<ref>{{cite book |last1 =Morgan |first1= B.  |last2 =Dolphin | first2 =D. | year =1987 | chapter=Synthesis and structure of biomimetic porphyrins. |editor-last=Buchler |editor-first=J.W.  |title=Metal Complexes with Tetrapyrrole Ligands I. Structure and Bonding, vol 64. |publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/BFb0036791 |isbn=978-3-540-17531-5}}</ref>
<ref>{{cite book |last1 =Baldwin |first1= J.E.  |last2 =Perlmutter | first2 =P. | year =1984  |chapter=Bridged, capped and fenced porphyrins. | pages=181–220 |editor1-last=Vögtle|editor1-first=J. F. |editor2-last= Weber |editor2-first=E.  |title=Host Guest Complex Chemistry III. Topics in Current Chemistry, vol 121. |publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/3-540-12821-2_6 |isbn=978-3-540-12821-2}}</ref>

=== Stereochemistry of enzymic reactions ===
The work described above is a subset of a broader field which attempts to understand the [[stereochemistry]] and [[Reaction mechanism|mechanism]] of [[enzyme catalysis]]. The Battersby group used their expertise in the use of [[radioactive tracer|tritium-labelled]] substrates to probe a number of enzyme systems, for example [[histidine decarboxylase]] and [[tyrosine decarboxylase]].<ref name=tritium/>

== Personal life ==
Battersby married Margaret Ruth née Hart in 1949. She was a [[botanist]] by profession who died of cancer in 1997. They had two sons, Martin and Stephen, four grandchildren and, after Margaret died, Alan acquired three great-grandchildren. In retirement, he enjoyed [[hiking]] and [[fly-fishing]] but he also kept in touch with his many colleagues and former students.<ref name=LaterLife/><ref name=TimesObituary/><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ch.cam.ac.uk/alumni/alan-battersby-obituary |title=Alan Battersby obituary |publisher=[[Department of Chemistry, University of Cambridge]] |last1=McDonald |first1=Ted |last2=Leeper |first2=Finian |access-date=2018-05-20}}</ref>

|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200220073843/https://www.liverpool.ac.uk/media/livacuk/cgso/committees/Honorary,Graduates,of,the,University.pdf |archive-date=2020-02-20 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
In 1988, he was elected a Foreign Honorary Member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]],<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|title=Book of Members, 1780-2010: Chapter B|url=http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterB.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160108175024/http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterB.pdf |archive-date=2016-01-08|publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|access-date=2025-10-01}}</ref> and a Foreign Fellow of the National Academy of Sciences of India in 1990. He was awarded the [[Wolf Prize in Chemistry]] along with [[Duilio Arigoni]] of [[ETH Zurich]] in 1989 for "their fundamental contributions to the elucidation of the mechanism of enzymic reactions and of the biosynthesis of natural products, in particular the pigments of life".<ref name=wolf>{{cite web |url=http://www.wolffund.org.il/index.php?dir=site&page=winners&cs=65&langpage=eng |title=The Wolf Prize in Chemistry |publisher=[[Wolf Foundation]]|access-date=2018-05-01}}</ref>

The Award of the [[Copley Medal]] of the [[Royal Society]] was made: {{centred pull quote|In recognition of his pioneering work in elucidating the detailed biosynthetic pathways to all the major families of plant alkaloids. His approach, which stands as a paradigm for future biosynthetic studies on complex molecules, combines isolation work, structure determination, synthesis, isotopic labelling and spectroscopy, especially advanced NMR, as well as genetics and molecular biology. This spectacular research revealed the entire pathway to vitamin B12.<ref name=Royal/>}}
